title: Participation Towards Authority: Community Agency, Local Governance and Planetary Health in a Rapidly Urbanising Tamil Nadu
content: Planetary health links human wellbeing to the ecological systems on which life depends, yet its governance dimension remains thinly examined. This paper argues that decisions about land, water, coastal resources and infrastructure determine both who benefits from environmental change and who bears its risks. Using a documentary, secondary-data case study of Tamil Nadu, India’s most urbanised large state (48.45% urban in 2011), it triangulates official, audit, peer-reviewed and media sources on the 2004 tsunami, Chennai’s floods and wetland loss, and the status of local government. Wetlands and water bodies in Chennai fell from 186.3 km² (1980) to 71.1 km² (2010) while built-up area rose from 47.6 to 402.1 km². Post-tsunami studies report limited participation in relocation decisions. Municipal own revenue is only 0.6% of GDP nationally, and rural local bodies were run by appointed officers after elected terms ended. The paper proposes a governance–resilience paradox: communities expected to be resilient often lack authority over the conditions on which resilience depends. It extends the “three Fs” of decentralisation with a fourth dimension, Voice, to define local agency.
